analysis.one_liner: Lets individuals pay a flat 20% income tax instead of the regular code.
analysis.headline: The bill had a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any taxpayer elect, each year, to pay a flat 20% tax on "FAIR taxable income" — gross income minus a few business deductions and a large standard deduction ($21,400 for couples, $10,700 for singles, plus $5,000 per child) — instead of calculating tax under the regular rate schedule. Anyone who would pay less under the flat option would switch, and the bill also required a three-fifths vote in each chamber for any future Congress to raise the flat rate or shrink the deduction. It never advanced past its committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose regular tax bill exceeds 20% of their FAIR taxable income would gain by electing the flat tax. The biggest winners are top-bracket earners, whose statutory rate now reaches 39.6% (the election replaces the top rate with 20%), though they give up itemized deductions such as mortgage interest. Some middle-income joint filers with children would also come out ahead, because the $21,400 joint deduction plus $5,000 per dependent is more generous than the regular standard deduction and personal exemptions for larger families.

how_it_helps.text: Gives every individual the option to pay a flat 20% rate on FAIR taxable income in place of the regular income tax, so top-bracket earners face a 20% rate rather than the current 39.6% top rate.

Sets a large standard deduction — $21,400 for joint filers, $14,000 for heads of household, $10,700 for singles, and $5,000 per dependent — which is indexed to inflation after 1998, benefiting larger families whose regular tax exceeds the flat alternative.

Simplifies filing for anyone who elects it: FAIR taxable income counts only the above-the-line deductions already allowed in computing adjusted gross income, so electors would not need to itemize deductions.

analysis.who_pays: Because the flat tax is elective, filers switch only when it lowers their bill, so the Treasury loses every dollar of the difference — with the largest losses concentrated among the highest earners — and the cost is spread to other taxpayers and future generations through higher deficits or the need for offsetting tax increases. Electors also give up itemized deductions (mortgage interest, charitable gifts, state and local taxes), and married couples would have to file jointly to use the option.
analysis.who_pays_short: Treasury and other taxpayers, via lost revenue

drawbacks.text: The tax is elective, so no one ever pays more under it — which means the entire cost is lost federal revenue, and the biggest gains go to the highest earners, who save the most by moving from the 39.6% top rate to 20%.

Section 3 locks in the terms: any future bill that raises the 20% rate, adds a rate bracket, or cuts the standard deduction could not even be considered in either chamber without a three-fifths vote, entrenching the tax cut against future Congresses.

Electors forfeit itemized deductions such as mortgage interest and charitable contributions, since FAIR taxable income allows only the deductions used to compute adjusted gross income — a real cost for homeowners and donors who itemize today.

Married couples could elect the flat tax only by filing a joint return (with an exception for spouses living apart), and parents would have to report the taxable income of children under 14 on their own return.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification and the option of a lower rate for some families are genuine, but the design is weighted toward the top: an elective flat tax guarantees revenue loss precisely among those least likely to need relief, and the three-fifths lock-in makes it hard for any later Congress to trim the rate or deduction to pay for it. For ordinary taxpayers, modest gains for larger joint filers would be outweighed by the revenue hole they eventually help fill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Rules committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Vince Snowbarger introduced the Flat Alternative Individual Return Tax Act of 1997 on October 21, 1997.
The House referred it that same day to the Ways and Means Committee and the Rules Committee, the standard first step for a tax bill.
The action record shows nothing further; the bill sat in committee until the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one moved ahead or behind in a material way: taxpayers' obligations stayed exactly as they were, the Treasury avoided the revenue loss the bill would have created, and the would-be chief beneficiaries — high earners who could have cut their rate to 20% — got nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody; the tax code stayed unchanged

for.name: Vince Snowbarger
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and made the case for an elective flat 20% individual tax.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax legislation (chaired that Congress by Rep. Bill Archer)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the only recorded support was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: An elective 20% flat rate replaces the 39.6% top statutory rate, so the biggest dollar savings go to the highest earners. Their gain comes out of federal revenue that other taxpayers and future generations would otherwise share.

industries.industry: Home-mortgage borrowers and the housing finance market
industries.note: Electors give up itemized deductions, including mortgage interest, which reduces the tax advantage of carrying a home loan. Some homeowners with large deductions would stay on the regular code rather than switch.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax advisory services
industries.note: For anyone who elects the flat return, filing needs only gross income, above-the-line deductions, and a standard deduction — no itemizing. Each voluntary switch shrinks the market for complex-return preparation.
